source.title: Universal YOCO for Efficient Depth Scaling
source.authors: Yu-Tao Sun; Li Dong; Tian-Zhu Ye; Shao-Han Huang; Jian-Yong Wang; Fu-Ru Wei

record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation-loss scaling across model sizes, training tokens, and compute in a different architecture and training setup; it also compares losses across depth/width layouts.
record.gate_note: The study reports loss-scaling results in Figures 2, 5, and 6 and layout comparisons in Table 5. Downstream benchmark scores, inference-efficiency results, and cited scaling-law findings are not rows because they do not directly measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper (YOCO-U). It tests scaling only incidentally. Section 4.4 sweeps YOCO and YOCO-U from 300M to 10.8B parameters at a fixed 20B tokens and states that the Kaplan scaling law 'empirically fits well'. That is a weak, figure-only V1 check in a new architecture. Table 5 compares a deeper/narrower layout against the baseline at equal parameter count, which bears on V4. No fitted exponents, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation or downstream-predictability analysis is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the layout sentence needs correcting. The authors say YOCO-U improves parameter utility and scaling behaviour while keeping a constant global KV cache and linear prefilling. On layout, they say training loss and downstream performance are almost irrelevant to model layout. This is said of the deep-vs-wide comparison in general, not of the deeper layout's own results, and they add that the recursion benefit persists on the deeper layout.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates YOCO and YOCO-U rather than reproducing the original scaling-law experiments; its reported sweeps use a specific architecture and training setup, with no fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The study compares non-recursive and recursive layouts and reports different LAMBADA perplexity outcomes for the non-recursive and recursive deeper-layout comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation loss improves as the recursive loop count rises from 1 to 5 in 1.3B YOCO-U.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing recursive computation in YOCO-U improves validation loss in the tested setup.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal FLOPs YOCO-U has lower loss than YOCO (ΔL=0.033). It also reaches YOCO's 210B-token loss with 80B tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture changes (partial recursion) shift the loss-versus-compute/token curve, improving compute and token efficiency.

record.problems: The scaling curves are largely reported as figures, with no fitted exponents, uncertainty estimates, or small-run extrapolation test. The parameter sweep uses 20B training tokens, and the evidence is confined to the study's architecture and setup.
record.rows_left_out: Downstream benchmark scores, inference throughput and cache results, and unrelated architecture comparisons are omitted because they do not measure the claim versions. Figure 6's loop-scaling result is retained under fits_no_version rather than linked to a version.

untested.parts: No fitted exponents. Token and compute dimensions are not tested as power laws. The parameter sweep spans only about 1.5 orders of magnitude at fixed tokens.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
Only one alternative aspect ratio is tested (40 layers × 1792 vs 20 × 2560) at 1.3B. Other shape factors are not tested.
Text pretraining only; the math SFT stage has no scaling analysis.
Downstream scores are reported at single scales and are not related to scale or loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: The authors' statement that training loss is almost irrelevant to layout (deep vs wide). No training-loss values are given, so it is text-only evidence for V4.
Loss vs activated parameters for YOCO and YOCO-U (MoE/recursive). The authors report the gap narrowing above 10B activated parameters.
Loss vs training tokens, 20B–300B, for each model separately (no power-law fit stated).

record.verdict_notes: Neither the V1 support nor the V4 support is strong. V1 rests on one sentence and a figure over about 1.5 orders of magnitude at fixed tokens; the 10.8B model at 20B tokens is likely data-limited. V4 rests on single 1.3B runs with no variance; LAMBADA perplexity diverges in the non-recursive case. The reader's V1 limits_scope label was dropped: missing exponents and range are untested parts, not qualifications.

versions.untested_parts: No fitted exponents are reported; the study does not establish power-law behavior over several orders of magnitude across general language-model setups.
The study does not fit laws on small runs and use them to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token allocation is reported.
The layout comparison covers the reported deeper-versus-wider variants, not a broad range of architectural choices.
No other modalities or training regimes are tested.
Downstream tasks are evaluated, but the study does not test whether their performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
The study reports no comparison of fitting choices or exponents, or evidence of curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: YOCO-U
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation loss as training FLOPs increased.
rows.note: The paper states this result for the equal-FLOPs comparison; loss-curve point values are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: This is a between-architecture comparison at equal FLOPs (YOCO-U vs YOCO, ΔL=0.033). It is not a test of whether loss follows a power law in compute. Record under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: YOCO-U
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation loss as training tokens increased.
rows.note: The paper describes the comparison as comparable performance; the curve values are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: This is a token-efficiency comparison between architectures (80B vs 210B tokens to equal loss). No power-law form is tested. It also runs under a constant LR schedule with no warmup.

rows.subject: YOCO-U
rows.operation_detail: Varied model parameter count and measured language-model loss.
rows.note: The authors state that the empirical scaling law fits well in this configuration and that YOCO-U gains consistently up to 6.4B parameters; plotted loss values are not given in text.
rows.check: The loop condition should be 3 (the default), not 'not stated'. The sweep covers only about 1.5 orders of magnitude (0.3B–10.8B) at a fixed 20B tokens, so data may bottleneck the larger models. Support rests on the authors' sentence 'scaling law... empirically fits well'; no exponents are given.

rows.subject: YOCO
rows.operation_detail: Varied model parameter count and measured language-model loss.
rows.note: The authors state that the empirical scaling law fits well in this configuration; plotted loss values are not given in text.
rows.check: The loop condition should be 1 (non-recursive YOCO). The same caveats as r3 apply: figure only, about 1.5 orders of magnitude, fixed 20B tokens, no fitted exponent.

conditions.value: non-recursive; doubled depth instead of width

rows.note: The deeper layout has substantially higher perplexity than the baseline.
rows.check: LAMBADA perplexity rises from 18.30 to 21.76 (about 19%) when depth is doubled at equal parameters. This is a target-word perplexity on a cloze task, not held-out pretraining loss. It is a single run with no uncertainty, so it is better read as layout sensitivity on one measure than as a clean absence.

relationships.condition: YOCO and YOCO-U parameter sweep 0.3B–10.8B, 20B tokens
relationships.reason: The authors state the Kaplan scaling law fits well and loss falls smoothly with size (r3, r4). The evidence is figure-only and covers a narrow range.
relationships.display_finding: Loss decreases smoothly with model size, and the Kaplan scaling law is reported to fit well over the narrow tested range.

relationships.condition: WikiText perplexity (both layouts) and LAMBADA perplexity (recursive layout), 1.3B, 20B tokens
relationships.reason: Doubling depth at equal parameters changes WikiText perplexity by under 2% (22.25→22.04; 21.01→21.42) and LAMBADA by under 1% in the recursive case (18.32→18.45) (r5, r7, r8). The authors also say training loss is 'almost irrelevant' to layout.
relationships.display_finding: Doubling depth changed WikiText perplexity from 22.25 to 22.04 and from 21.01 to 21.42, both under 2%, while recursive-layout LAMBADA perplexity changed from 18.32 to 18.45, under 1%.

relationships.condition: LAMBADA perplexity, non-recursive deep vs wide YOCO
relationships.reason: LAMBADA perplexity worsens from 18.30 to 21.76 with the deeper layout, so the small-effect claim does not hold on this measure (r6).
relationships.display_finding: The deeper layout increased LAMBADA perplexity from 18.30 to 21.76.
